Plan, knit and complete an Ear Flap Hat. This collection is designed for all knitters, no matter what your skill level.
Included is the Ear Flap Hat Collection of patterns
More than just a rectangle, this hat isn't hard to knit. The plan is to take it step-by-step. The goal is to FINISH
  • Choose your size
  • Choose your yarn
  • Plan YOUR design (no changes mid-stream)
  • Focus on each section
  • Learn/practice techniques
  • FINISH your hat

Are you NEW?
Knit the pattern "as is" focusing on learning/perfecting techniques used for the design. Don't over-complicate things.
The goal is to FINISH the hat, learn and practice new techniques and build your confidence with your machine
We suggest you knit one of gathered crown styles.
Ready for an adventure?
Use this simple pattern as a canvas for your creativity.
Challenge yourself to try a new-to-you stitch pattern technique. How about Fairisle?
How about combining hand and machine knitting?
Because the shaping is basic, you can focus on the new technique and expand your skills.

Don't forget the Knit it Now 2020 Hat challenge

Knit for charity and WIN.

You are making progress! ... we've spent a lot of time planning, practicing and thinking about knitting ... are you ready to do some "real knitting"?

DON'T SKIP THIS SECTION!

Your success with this course AND your success with your knitting machine depends on your understanding and mastering the art of knitting gauge swatches.
Without a swatch we are knitting in the dark.
  • How is the final sweater going to feel in the yarn and stitch pattern you've chosen?
  • Do you have enough yarn?
  • Do you have enough needles on your machine for the size you chose?
PLUS you must know YOUR gauge to create your custom pattern
Do you struggle with swatching? Can you knit to the correct size every time?
You need the complete Swatching Course
FREE for subscribers

SWATCHING IS NOT OPTIONAL

blocks.title: Step 1: Your Success Depends on this

components.html:
If you haven't used your chosen yarn before, how do you know the best tension to knit your blanket? 
Knitters tend to use the terms "tension swatch" and "gauge swatch" interchangeably, lets take a look at both.

GAUGE SWATCH

The gauge swatch is the "official" swatch used when designing a garment.
It is knit at a specific size, marked for accurate stitch and row measurement and "dressed" as the final garment will be treated.
TIP: Whatever method you use to create a swatch, the key is to correctly measure it and calculate your gauge.

TENSION SWATCH

(AKA "Get Acquainted Swatch)
When I pick up a new cone of yarn, I can't wait to thread up my machine and see what the yarn looks like.   From the initial cast on, I start guessing what setting on my tension dial I need to use.  I knit a few inches and reach down and start to feel the resulting fabric.
Once I get a feel for the yarn (what machine, general tension setting at stockinette, etc) I create a tension swatch.  This helps me fine-tune the tension needed to achieve the fabric I like and allows me to play with various techniques.  I'm often very surprised that a yarn looks great in tuck, and awful in slip, for example.  Adding a few eyelets here and there tells me if the yarn will work up in lace.
Let's practice knitting a tension swatch.

1. Play!
  2. Start knitting stockenette at the tightest tension that will knit.  (If the tension is too tight, you'll see stitches that don't form properly.
  3. Knit 2-4 inches. Knit a marker row (change colors, work a few eyelets across the row or knit a sewing thread in with the main yarn)
  4. Keep knitting sections, marking the tension dial number in each section.  Knit the last section as loosely as possiblle, even if you think this will be too loose ... I'm often very pleasantly surprised at the result.
  5. Transfer every other needle to out of work postion and knit a section - put all needles back into work.
  6. Work a simple tuck, or slip, or any stitch pattern of your choice ... base your tension dial setting on the stockinette sections you just knit.
The point of this exercise is to put the yarn through it's paces ... ignite your creativity, and get a feel for what the yarn can do.  If you don't have a huge cone, you can always re-wind this knitting. At this point, you probably know exactly what you want to do with this yarn.  Knit your Gauge Swatch, dress it and and you are ready to design and knit your sweater.

blocks.title: Step 2: Gauge swatch verses Tension Swatch

components.html:
Hand knitters use the excuse "It takes too much time to knit a swatch", then they are often disappointed that their knitting doesn't fit.
Machine knitters, rejoice!  Knitting a swatch is fast and the information it supplies is invaluable ...even for something as simple as a blanket.

Ear Flap hats are worn differently than other hat styles.
Take a few minutes to review these differences BEFORE you size your pattern

slides.caption: The body of an Ear Flap Hat needs to be shorter than the other styles.

1. Measure the circumference (not too tight, but snug enough to stay on in the wind)
  2. Determine the desired length (long enough to cover the ears, extra long for fashion)
Without Ear Flaps, the hat needs to be long enough to cover the ears.  It can also be adjustable by folding up the brim
The body of an Ear Flap Hat doesn't cover the ears.  It also rides higher on the head, exposing more of the face and neck.
The body of an Ear Flap Hat needs to be shorter than the other styles.

Considering how this hat is worn, adjust your Perfect Fit pattern with your measurements.
Also consider the position of the flaps as you re-hang them on the machine. Measure to make sure the flaps cover the ears.

components.html: The pattern suggests decreasing 3 stitches from the edge of the flap and allowing the edge to roll. Use whatever decrease method you like.

Knit doubled ear flaps in one piece, using short row shaping
  • Scrap on according to your pattern
  • Knit straight as instructed (for length)
  • Shape the flap with short row decreases and increases
  • Knit straight as instructed
  • Pick up the live cast on stitches
  • Knit 1 row
  • Scrap off
When it comes time to re-hang the flaps on the machine:
  • If you knit the extra row, notice the purl bumps and identify the public and private sides of the flaps.
  • You may choose to rip out the extra row after re-hanging the flaps
Finishing:
Neatly seam the straight edges
Options:
If you prefer a less pointed flap, knit fewer rows in the short row decrease/increase sections. Be sure to add rows to the straight section for overall flap length
Ties:
  • Pick up 3-4 stitches from the "point" of the flap and knit I-Cord ties.
  • OR Knit the I-Cord and neatly stitch to the points
By starting the flap with an open cast on, you can rehang the live stitches on the needlebed, then cast on and knit the body of the hat for a seam less join.

sections.title: Tip 1: Right and Wrong Side
sections.bodyHtml:
When re-hanging the flaps take care to hang them with the wrong side (private side) facing.
If you look closely in the image above, My flaps are hanging with the right side (public side) facing.
I chose to work a few rows of garter stitch (with a garter bar) between the ear flap and hat body.

sections.title: Tip 2: Re-Hang Cast on Stitches
sections.bodyHtml: Have you ever noticed that when you rehang the cast on stitches (hung hem or these earflaps) there is one less stitch than you cast on? Mystery solved! Watch and see why.

sections.title: Tip 3: Modified Cast On
sections.bodyHtml:
After rehanging the ear flaps, you may want to ONLY cast on over the empty needles. In other words, if you are working an e-wrap cast on for the hat edge, don't e-wrap over the flap needles. This will ensure uninterrupted knitting between the flap and the body of the hat.
Notice in the image above, there are green Cast on Rags over the hat edge needles and the flap stitches are hung and ready to knit.

sections.title: Tip 4: Hem Options
sections.bodyHtml:
Design your own pattern by choosing an optional cuff for the hat body.
  1. Simply E-wrap cast on and let the hem roll
  2. Work an e-wrap cast on and knit a few rows BEFORE hanging the ear flaps
  3. Hang the ear flaps, then cast on in ribbing. Knit 1-3" in ribbing, then transfer the stitches to the stitch pattern of your choice
  4. Cast on and hang a hem BEFORE hanging the ear flaps
  5. Knit a simple (stretchy) cast on and finish the brim edge with crochet
  6. knit a simple (stretchy) cast on and finish the brim edge with I-cord

sections.title: Tip 5: Ties
sections.bodyHtml:
• We used I-Cord for our samples
  • If you crochet, you may want to crochet the ties
  • Consider a Twisted Cord for the ties
  • Add a small pompom to the ends of the ties

blocks.title: Join the Flaps to the Hat

components.html:
If you choose to knit a hung hem for the lower edge of your hat

When building your pattern be sure to add to the length "E".
In other words, if you want your finished hat to be 10" with a 1" hem, build your pattern so "E" equals 11"

Knit a hem and insert the earflaps

  1. Cast on with waste yarn and ravel cord (open cast on)
  2. Knit the desired hem depth (1st half of the hem)
  3. Knit a turning row
  4. Remove the knitting from the machine (scrap off or garter bar)
  5. Hang the flaps according to the pattern (Note the public and private sides)
  6. Rehang the hem stitches
  7. Knit the 2nd half of the band
  8. Pick up the open hem stitches to complete the hem
  9. Continue knitting the hat

Although the following images show the doubled ear flaps, the single ear flaps can be inserted in a hung hem in exactly the same manner

slides.caption:
• The ear flaps were knit separately and scrapped off. Notice the orange scrap yarn.
  • The hung hem was started with waste yarn (orange) and ravel cord
  • The ear flaps were inserted in the hem turning row
  • The hem was then completed and picked up
Start by knitting the first half of the band (not shown). I removed the band on a garter bar, but you could use a circular hand knitting needle or scrap off.

Position the ear flaps with the PRIVATE (wrong) side facing.
I suggest you remove the waste yarn to confirm all the stitches have been picked up.
Rehang the first half of the band OVER the flaps. Make sure the PRIVATE (wrong) side is facing)
Knit the 2nd half of the hem
Pick up the open cast on stitches to close the hem. I recommend removing the waste yarn to confirm that all the stitches have been picked up.
Knit the remainder of the hat
The flaps are inserted in the turning row of the hem.

components.html: Although this classic crown top style is a bit tedious on the knitting machine, the resulting fit and decorative swirl are well worth the effort!

Each gore is worked individually and shaped with decreases. Plain or fancy decrease ... it's up to you!
Remember to work your decreases so there is a seaming stitch on the edge for neat seaming.

slides.caption:
No matter what crown style, here are some fun embellishments for your hat tops.

Yarn Pompoms are classic.

Crochet corkscrews add a touch of whimsey.

Gather the top and add a ruffle for a fast finish!

  1. Knit the desired length of the hat
  2. Create a row of eyelets transferring every other stitch to it's neighbor
  3. Knit for 1" - 1½"
  4. Bind off
  5. Run a ribbon or I-cord thru the eyelets to gather

Make a loopy top:
1. Knit a length of I-Cord 10"-12" long .....
2. Gather the cord into loops and attach it to the top of the hat

"Dreadlocks" can be fun!
1. Knit a long length of I-Cord .....

2. Tie knots every 4" - 6"
3. Cut between the knots
4. Gather and attach the strands to the top of the hat
Fellow knitter, Hope, shared her cute-as-can-be hat finished with a top knot.
Here's another with a smaller knot.

1. Knit your hat for the desired length less about 1"
  2. Transfer every other needle, putting the empty needles out of work
  3. Knit for 1"
  4. Create eyelets by transferring every other needle, keeping the emptied needles in working position
  5. Hope reduced the bulk by transferring again, then moving all the stitches, filling the empty needles
  6. Knit for about 1"
  7. Bind off
Run a cord through the eyelets

Pull the cord tight and fasten to form the knot.

Voila! A fast, fun embellishment to finish your gathered hat

Thank you, Hope, for the inspiration!
